subtitle: Using short but strong elliptic curve keys to sign and encrypt messages.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needs strong public-key cryptography for digital signatures and key exchange, but elliptic curve algorithms offer smaller keys than RSA while maintaining equivalent security.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3278 defines how to use elliptic curve algorithms (ECDSA for signatures, ECDH and ECMQV for key agreement) with CMS SignedData, EnvelopedData, and AuthenticatedData structures, following standards like ANSI X9.62 and IEEE 1363.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now use elliptic curve cryptography in CMS for more efficient and secure message protection. This RFC was replaced by RFC 5753, which provides an updated profile.

today: RFC 3278 is an Informational document that was replaced by RFC 5753 in January 2010. It described how to use elliptic curve cryptography algorithms (ECDSA, ECDH, ECMQV) within CMS for digital signatures and encrypted messages.

sections.title: ECC in Cryptographic Messages
sections.content:
RFC 3278 specifies how to use Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) algorithms within the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), a standard format for cryptographically signed and encrypted messages. The RFC defines profiles for three main CMS content types: SignedData (digital signatures using ECDSA), EnvelopedData (encryption using ECDH or ECMQV key agreement), and AuthenticatedData (authentication using ECMQV).

ECC provides equivalent security to RSA with significantly smaller key sizes—for example, a 256-bit elliptic curve key offers comparable security to a 2048-bit RSA key. The specification is based on ANSI X9.62, IEEE 1363, and the SEC (Standards for Efficient Cryptography) standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Elliptic curve math is a smarter way to do cryptography: your secret keys can be shorter but still just as secure. This document explains how to use it for signing and encrypting messages.

sections.title: SignedData with ECDSA and Key Agreement
sections.content:
For digital signatures, the RFC specifies the use of the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), which is the elliptic curve analog of DSA. When using ECDSA with CMS SignedData, the digest algorithm MUST be SHA-1, and the signature algorithm identifier is ecdsa-with-SHA1.

For encrypted messages, the RFC defines two main approaches: ephemeral-static ECDH and 1-Pass ECMQV. Ephemeral-static ECDH uses a temporary ephemeral key pair for the sender and the recipient's long-term static key to agree on a shared secret. One-Pass ECMQV uses three key pairs (ephemeral and static for both sender and recipient) and can be used with both EnvelopedData and AuthenticatedData, providing mutual authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: To sign a message, you use elliptic curve math to create a cryptographic stamp. To encrypt, you and the receiver use it to secretly agree on a key to encrypt your message.

sections.title: Message Processing and AuthenticatedData
sections.content:
The sending agent for ECDSA computes a message digest according to CMS standards and then applies the ECDSA signature method from ANSI X9.62, encoding the result as an ECDSA-Sig-Value structure containing two integers (r and s). The receiving agent verifies the signature using the same standards.

For EnvelopedData, the sending agent obtains the recipient's EC public key and domain parameters, generates an ephemeral key pair, performs the key agreement operation, and obtains a shared secret used to encrypt the content-encryption key. For AuthenticatedData with 1-Pass ECMQV, the mechanism is similar but provides authentication and integrity protection without non-repudiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender creates the signature or encrypted key, and the receiver uses math to verify it or decrypt the message.

sections.title: Recommended Algorithms and Security
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support either SignedData with ECDSA or EnvelopedData with ephemeral-static ECDH. SHOULD support both. Interoperability is encouraged by using elliptic curve domain parameters specified by ANSI X9.62, NIST FIPS-186-2, and the SECG SEC2 standard. ECC certificates follow X.509 standards with ECC-specific algorithms.

The security of ECC depends on the difficulty of the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, proper random-number generation for ephemeral keys, and secure distribution of public keys. Key sizes MUST match the security level needed; 256-bit curves provide security equivalent to 2048-bit RSA. Senders can announce ECC support to receivers using the SMIMECapabilities attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: To make sure different systems can work together, everyone should use the same elliptic curves and algorithms from published standards. Make sure to use enough key bits and get your random numbers from a good source.
